body:
This is probably a duplicate of:
* https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86926

@AThousandShips

The other thread doesn't specifically address the problem with the C# garbage collector being suppressed. The issues are closely related and I can see this causing a lot of problems related to memory.

The garbage collection of the wrapper objects in the example code is prevented by the code allocating but never freeing the `GodotObject`s, so the native objects stick around, as do their (cached) C# wrappers. The wrappers will be disposed/finalized once the underlying native objects are freed.

As for how working with Godot objects that use an ownership model instead of reference counting could be made more intuitive for C# programmers, that is indeed being discussed in the issue linked above.

I've noticed that the C# garbage collector gets blamed as if it's operating slowly. People think they're waiting for it to catch up, when it's effectively disabled for all the built-in Godot types.

Godot's in-house garbage collector (`RefCounted`) has to run first, or the objects have to be freed manually. It leads to strange advice, like calling `GC.Collect()` manually to try and speed it up, when it will never run on Godot types until Godot frees them.

There's probably a very good reason why it was designed that way for GDScript. For C#, there might be some benefits to giving control back to the dotnet GC if that works with the engine architecture. For example, [a cyclic reference will not be freed automatically](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_refcounted.html) with Godot's `RefCounted`, but [C# doesn't have that problem](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/8840567/garbage-collector-and-circular-reference).

I think there may be some misunderstanding about how Godot's .NET interop works. Godot is a C++ engine and, as such, .NET doesn't know anything about the native objects and the GC is not directly responsible from freeing those.

What our C# wrappers try to do is ensure that native objects remain valid as long as there's a managed C# reference to them.

> Memory is the scarce resource being allocated, so that's what should be cleaned up. Calling `Dispose()` should do the same thing as calling `Free()`.
> Based on my testing, `Dispose()` only removes the handle to the unmanaged object. This is why memory leaks.

You are correct that `Dispose()` only releases the managed handle. It won't destroy the native object, unless the object is `RefCounted` and the count reaches 0. You are expected to free non-`RefCounted` objects manually.

> // automatically release engine resources when the GC picks 
> // up the managed one. this is what Dispose is intended for.
> // you don't need a separate ref counter on the engine side.

The native object may still be referenced by C++, GDScript, or any other scripting language. If you free the native object, you are destroying it for everyone. So this approach only works for objects that C# owns. Otherwise, it could lead to use-after-free bugs for any other part of the engine still holding a reference.

Imagine that you get a reference to a `Label` in a C# script, you set the `Text` property, and then dispose it since you are done with the Node in C#. If you free the Node it will also be removed from the scene tree, and anything else still referencing that `Label` would then be operating on a freed object.

Now think of a file. If I open a file in C#, write to it, and then dispose it. I expect the file to still exist in the filesystem. The C# `Dispose()` method just closes the handle, it doesn't delete the file.

I think @bs-mwoerner describes this better in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86926#issuecomment-1880837883 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86926#issuecomment-1881417972

> The other thread doesn't specifically address the problem with the C# garbage collector being suppressed.

I don't know what you mean by this. Could you please clarify? I don't really see how this issue is different from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86926.

> It leads to strange advice, like calling `GC.Collect()` manually to try and speed it up.

We don't recommend using `GC.Collect()` in production. We sometimes ask users in GitHub issues to use it to check if there's actually a memory leak, because often users confuse a memory leak with the GC not releasing memory immediately. But it should not be necessary to use `GC.Collect()` in production.

As far as I understand it (as a user), as soon as you use `GodotObject` or any derivative, you are basically giving ownership of the object to the engine and dotnet only handles the wrapper. dotnet does not know how the object is used in the engine and if might be 'back-called' at some point. As the others have mentioned, this is why you can't free it just because there is no dotnet reference. But it also means that you can't collect the dotnet object, in case it might be called by the engine.
Think of a script that is attached to a node but nowhere referenced in your C# code. In this case it would be immediately collected after it was initialized and the engine would not be able to reference the object to call, e.g., `_Process` or signal handlers or get it with `GetNode` or similar later. From this standpoint it makes sense that the engine keeps the dotnet object alive.

I think it it worth discussing if it makes sense that `GodotObject` is disposable at all as is mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86926#issuecomment-2872629756. I don't know in which case one would want to dispose the wrapper and keep the engine object alive, but maybe there are some cases.

> This is an earthshattering catastrophe coz u end up with threads https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/107518 with the gentleman @Joy-less bullying a poor, innocent C# dev who's just trying to do his job. He probably doesn't even know that it's bullying. @Joy-less is telling him that it's all C#'s fault, and if only it had a reference counter like the wonderful GDScript it would all be ok.

The thread you linked does not seem to be related since `Array` does not have a strong gc-handle that prevents any garbage collection (maybe I'm missing something?).

> RefCounted is simply an inferior, homebrew GC that's forced to run before the optimized Microsoft version can do its work.

I woudn't call `RefCounted` and inferior dotnet GC. It is used for automatic memory management in the engine where the dotnet reference can be just one of many.

> That's the problem. Control is taken away from C# and given to the 'native'. It's backwards.

Godot is a C++ engine, not a C# engine. The .NET runtime is a guest, not the host. There are reasons for that, and as far as I understand, that's a fundamental design decision of the engine.

Reference counting is a common and relatively simple programming technique in C++ and isn't only there for GDScript. In fact, Godot (unofficially) supports all kinds of programming languages through GDExtension, such as Rust, Go, D, Swift or Odin. Some languages have their own GC or entirely different strategies for memory management, so the control is exactly where it belongs: in the engine on the C++ side.

> We can see the big picture.

To me it rather looks like all you see is C# (and its admittedly quite lacking implementation).

The Godot development team often preferred usability, accessibility and simplicity over highly optimized code or cutting edge features. That's exactly why it's so widespread, adaptable and easy to use. There are countless addons written in GDScript, C++ or other languages, relying on the Godot core and its memory management strategy.


Sidenote: 
Calling GDScript users monkeys (even metaphorically) is highly unprofessional and sounds concerning to me in combination with your username and other metaphors you've used so far. Maybe you should rethink how you deal with other people's goals and opinions first before you trumpet your own.

I can see that the conversation went a little "spicy" so to say and then has gone quiet for a bit, but I'm a new explorer of the engine source code and memory management and language interop is of particular interest to me, so feel free to correct me if I'm wrong, but I just want to see if I understand the situation correctly. I'm by no means an expert in either C++ or C#, so I might get the philosophy wrong, feel free to correct me on that as well.

I'm listing all of the assumptions I'm going off of here, it's just what I could gather from the repository:

_Sidenote: I know these are classes but I'm speaking of instance behaviour_

- `Object` is memory-managed by C++ and the Godot engine
- `GodotObject` is a C# object holding what is essentially a pointer to the C++ `Object`
- For `GodotObject` to function fully, upon allocation and use, it may modify the pointed-to C++ `Object` in a way where the `GodotObject` allocates additional unmanaged memory in order to allow `Object` to communicate with `GodotObject`.
- `GodotObject.Dispose` ensures that the extra allocated unmanaged memory is freed, "detaching" from the `Object` in the process.
- No aforementioned point can be used in any way to describe `Object`'s allocation/freeing.
- Newly allocated `Objects` are initially only accessible and freeable by the allocating function.
- `GodotObject.Free()` is automatically generated and simply calls `Object.free()` of the pointed-to `Object`
- `new GodotObject()` and `GodotObject.new()` does allocate a new unmanaged `Object`

This means that essentially:

- `GodotObject` is more akin to a separately existing non-owning Adapter structure. It is useful as long as something connects on both ends, but either end can send data and program flow bidirectionally when necessary.
- Thus `GodotObject` doesn't have unmanaged memory cleanup in the traditional sense what a C# dev could expect from a C# library.
- `Free` and `new` have been imported either by convenience and for similarity to GDScript, not C# principles in mind.
- There exists a lack of allocation parity between the constructor and destructor. Constructor can allocate unmanaged memory, which the destructor won't free by itself. 

I think a lot of the confusion has stemmed because it's just that: an endpoint for which C# can connect to.

And because it is just an adapter, the same non-deterministic memory-ownership issue bled into C#. Not to say this is bad, in some cases experienced devs might use this to their advantage, but this is an issue that can arise in any similar C# project.  As far as I can tell, saying the devil's name won't get me banned, but even Unity has this same issue with resource loading and unloading.

But the last point I realized just now while writing the next 2 paragraphs. The lack of allocation parity is actually one of the biggest flaws in this. It's a common thing in C++ to have the rule that "`new` must be accompanied by `delete`", "`new[]` has a `delete[]`", "`malloc` has a `free`". In C#, you'd have the constructor and Dispose. (Technically there's a deconstructor as well, but we'll ignore that).

But I can relate with C# users in this case. `GodotObjects` are very common (almost as if they are the cornerstone of the whole project :P) and having to think about how their memory is managed is something C# users won't be accustomed to. It will inevitably lead to a lot of frustration, fracture the community and damage the initiative of maintaining C#. It is the only other actively maintained language apart from GDScript (the original coding language for the engine) and C++ (the language the engine runs on). And as an officially maintained language, I do believe we should improve it so this wouldn't be such a hot button issue.

_Hard speculation._

I don't know how feasible it is in the current ecosystem, but one naive solution to this issue would be to expand on the C# side to clear up potential pitfalls with the current system. Leave the current `GodotObject` as just that: an adapter. Anyone who uses it has to be careful that whatever they do can mess up memory management.
On top of it, we can maybe create a `ManagedGodotObject`.

`ManagedGodotObject` means the C# `GodotObject` has full ownership of the underlying `Object` instance and is allowed to deallocate it as it pleases. Because I work under the assumption that the instance isn't accessible from anywhere else, as long as you don't do any actions that transfer ownership (like adding to a scene tree), it should be fine..? If it still causes memory issues then in all likelihood it'd be some GDScript code that doesn't assume correct ownership. If one calls a function that transfers ownership explicitly, the `ManagedGodotObject` would internally change its state to as if it deallocated it. It can still provide access to the `GodotObject`

`GodotObject` would be similar to how it currently is. With the removal of the default constructor to have allocation parity.


This took me far longer than it should have to write and this is probably a dead thread already, but eh, whatever, have fun with my ramblings.
Maybe what you want is a C# version Godot, not Godot with mono.

I mean... Yeah...
Yes in the sense that I want a C# API which doesn't require manual memory management which has similar, but different semantics of the one that is built in the standard framework (`IDisposable`), while using the standard one in a way that isn't intuitive from a C# development perspective. At least holding an owning/non-owning flag that is used in Dispose is better.
